profile.summary: DEKOIS 2.0 is a virtual screening benchmark: for each target it asks how well a method ranks experimentally validated active compounds above property-matched decoys. The official page offers 81 target sets for download; Shen et al. describe each set as 40 actives from BindingDB and 1200 decoys selected from ZINC. It is used by developers of docking, scoring and co-folding methods to compare enrichment of actives.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark measures early recognition in structure-based virtual screening: given a protein target and a library of 40 known actives mixed with 1200 decoys, can a method place the actives near the top of its ranking. Because the decoys are chosen to match the actives' physicochemical properties, a method cannot succeed simply by preferring, for example, heavier or more lipophilic molecules. Shen et al. use it as their primary reference set for comparing AlphaFold3-like co-folding methods with conventional docking programs.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each target set pairs actives taken from BindingDB with decoys selected from ZINC and matched on molecular properties, giving an actives-to-decoys ratio of 1 to 30. The official page lists 81 targets, spread across kinases, proteases, nuclear receptors, GPCRs and other enzyme families, and offers the target sets in three download parts plus a ligands download. The page does not print a version string, a licence or a construction protocol; the construction details on this page come from Shen et al.'s description. Shen et al. also used the protein templates and initial ligand conformers that come with the dataset rather than preparing their own.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a ranking of each target's library. Shen et al. score rankings with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), BEDROC with alpha = 80.5, which weights the top 2% of the ranking to 80% of the score, and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%. Per-target values are then summarised across targets, with the mean marked in their box plots. Their comparison runs on 79 of the 81 targets, because two targets (pygl-in and pygl-out) were dropped as too costly to model; values for one tool, SurfDock, were taken over from earlier work and cover all 81 targets. There is no central leaderboard: each paper publishes its own numbers.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None. The benchmark is a screening set only: every compound of a target is ranked and scored, with no train, validation or test division.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets' and 'Evaluation metrics'

quotes.text: EFx%, defined as the ratio of true positives found in the top x% of ranked compounds relative to random selection

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC, BEDROC (alpha = 80.5) and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%, as used by Shen et al.; higher is better for all of them. AUROC runs from 0 for complete failure through 0.5 for random to 1 for perfect classification.

quotes.text: The corresponding AUROC value ranges from 0 (complete failure) to 0.5 (random prediction) to 1 (perfect classification).
We evaluated EF at 0.5%, 1%, and 5% thresholds to capture performance across different screening depths.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: As reported by Shen et al.: five docking programs (Glide SP, AutoDock Vina, GOLD CHEMPLP, Surflex-Dock, LeDock) and five machine-learning docking tools (Gnina, TankBind, KarmaDock, CarsiDock, SurfDock), with the values for all but AF3, Protenix, Boltz-2 and Gnina taken over from earlier studies.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Evaluation of AF3's built-in confidence scores on DEKOIS2.0 dataset'; Fig. 1 caption

quotes.text: we compared these approaches with five popular traditional docking programs (Glide SP, AutoDock Vina, GOLD CHEMPLP, Surflex-Dock, and LeDock) and five emerging AI-powered docking tools (Gnina, TankBind, KarmaDock, CarsiDock and SurfDock)
The results for approaches except AF3, Protenix, Boltz-2 and Gnina were directly retrieved from previous studies

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None in the benchmark itself, and Shen et al. warn that it is a problem here: the set was released over ten years before their study and its template structures may overlap AlphaFold3's training data, so they built the separate GPCRrecent set. They also say Boltz-2's affinity numbers on DEKOIS2.0 are likely over-estimated, because Boltz-2 took affinity data from the same public databases that DEKOIS 2.0 draws on. In place of a split control they computed, for each active compound, its minimum Tanimoto similarity (ECFP4) to any PDB ligand, as the paper words it, and re-calculated the metrics at varying similarity thresholds.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Results on ligand similarity

quotes.text: DEKOIS2.0 had been released over ten years and its template protein structures might exhibit a significant overlap with AF3's training data
its reported performance metrics are likely significantly over-estimated due to this data overlap
We then performed identical fingerprint calculations for each active compound in DEKOIS2.0 and thus determined their minimum Tanimoto similarity to any PDB ligand.
For varying similarity thresholds, we re-calculated the performance metrics for each screening tool.
Our analysis began by retrieving all PDB ligands used in Protenix training and calculating their ECFP4 fingerprints

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No replicates or intervals are asked for. Shen et al. report the spread across targets with box plots and mark the mean; the co-folding predictions were run with one fixed random seed (seed = 1).
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Fig. 1 caption; Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

quotes.text: White squares in box plots indicate mean values for each metric.
five predictions were generated using a fixed random seed (seed = 1)

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A compound in a target's screening library, labelled active or decoy; one score is produced per target.

quotes.text: 40 experimentally-validated active compounds from BindingDB and 1200 property-matched decoys selected from ZINC

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated in the files read. The official page lists protein targets by name, including human proteins and pathogen proteins such as HIV-1 protease and the SARS coronavirus 3C-like protease, but no species column is printed.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: The actives carry measured binding or inhibition data from BindingDB. The decoys are not assayed: they are library compounds matched on properties, which Shen et al. call artificially generated decoys.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

quotes.text: 40 experimentally-validated active compounds from BindingDB
the negative samples in both the DEKOIS2.0 and GPCRrecent datasets are artificially-generated decoys, which might introduce potential bias

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not fixed by the benchmark. The dataset ships protein templates and initial ligand conformers, so methods may use the 3D structure; Shen et al. note that co-folding methods take only one-dimensional protein and ligand sequences, while some baselines need 3D structural information.

quotes.text: While AF3-like approaches feed only one-dimensional sequences for both proteins and ligands as inputs, some structure-based baseline methods employed in this study require 3D structural information.
we used the provided well-established protein templates and initial ligand conformers

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot screening in practice: in Shen et al. the methods are run as released, with default or recommended settings, and nothing is trained on the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

quotes.text: All other parameters remained at their default or recommended values.

strengths.text: The actives are experimentally validated measurements from BindingDB, and the decoys are matched on physicochemical properties, so simple property bias does not by itself produce enrichment.

strengths.text: 81 target sets spanning many protein families are downloadable from the official page, with the protein templates and ligand conformers included, so methods that need a prepared structure can be run without extra preparation.

limitations.text: The negatives are property-matched library compounds, not assayed inactives. Shen et al. report that a reviewer raised this as a possible bias, which is why they added a LIT-PCBA subset where actives and inactives are both measured.

notes: This page is written from the official download page and from Shen et al.'s description, because the DEKOIS 2.0 primary paper is closed access and not in PMC. Shen et al.'s article is licensed CC BY-NC 3.0, which is not one of the short identifiers this format allows, so the source carries no licence field and its bytes are not stored. Two sizes are recorded separately: 81 targets on the official page and 79 in Shen et al.'s comparison. Per-target active and decoy counts beyond the 40 and 1200 figures were not read. Records 12 (GPCRrecent) and 13 (LIT-PCBA) share the Shen et al. source with this one; the shared facts are written from the same passages.
